author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Build a per-game PS2 performance budget
summary: Define target emulation speed, frame-time reserve, thermal duration, resolution, accuracy, and battery conditions for one title, then accept a profile only when its worst known scenes remain inside the recorded limits.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 benchmark chart comparing average and low-percentile performance measurements

blocks.text: Turn acceptable play into measurable limits

A performance budget states what the profile must sustain instead of endlessly chasing the highest resolution. For one title, record target emulation speed, worst acceptable frame-time behavior, minimum run duration before thermal decline, visual correctness requirements, battery or plugged state, and a small reserve. Anchor the budget to representative saves rather than a generic emulator menu.
Do not fund extra resolution by disabling a correctness feature the game requires. Visual acceptance and timing acceptance belong in the same budget.

items: Three saves covering light, typical, and worst-known workload.
A verified visual baseline at native resolution and safe accuracy.
A target session duration and documented device power condition.
Frame-time, emulation-speed, audio, and thermal observations.
A baseline per-game profile that can be restored exactly.
1. Measure all three scenes at the correct native-resolution baseline.
2. Write the minimum acceptable emulation speed and pacing for each checkpoint.
3. Add one resolution step and rerun the worst scene through the target duration.
4. Add optional visual features one at a time only while timing reserve remains.
5. Reject a setting when late-session speed, audio, or correctness crosses the budget.
6. Repeat the last passing profile from a cool start and a warm start.
7. Record device, firmware, driver, game region, and emulator version with the result.
8. Save the accepted values per game and schedule retesting only after relevant changes.

blocks.text: The worst-scene requirement prevents a visually impressive opening from defining the profile. A reserve absorbs random load, warmer ambient conditions, and later effects without running at the edge. Per-game storage avoids forcing one title's expensive settings onto the rest of the library.
The profile passes when every required scene and condition remains within both correctness and timing limits.

items: Light, typical, and heavy checkpoints are documented.
Sustained duration reaches the thermal steady state.
Audio, frame pacing, and visual correctness all pass.
The final profile succeeds from both cool and warm starts.
At least one step of practical timing reserve remains.
Only peak FPS is specified: add sustained and low-percentile behavior.
The heavy save is not reproducible: replace it with a deterministic route.
A system update changes clocks or driver: create a new dated result.
The budget ignores battery state: define the intended daily condition.

blocks.text: Return to the last accepted budget profile

Restore the recorded renderer, resolution, accuracy, speed, and synchronization values, remove experimental overrides, and validate the worst checkpoint once. Preserve rejected test rows so the same marginal settings are not rediscovered later.

The same title and settings can have different reserve on another SoC, firmware, ambient temperature, or display mode. Copy the method between devices, not the final multiplier or timing threshold. Reserve is also scene-dependent: build the budget around a repeatable demanding area, then verify menus, effects-heavy battles, video playback, and a sustained session. A profile that barely passes one benchmark has no margin for radio activity, charging heat, or background work and should be labeled experimental rather than stable.
